blindness.how: the grades were written from a review pack that carried no judge output: scripts/blind_worksheet.py extracts the queue through a field allow-list and re-checks its own output for any grade-shaped key before writing it
blindness.grades_unchanged_since: the annotations in tools/review/baseline_*.json were not edited after the judge's grades existed
blindness.what_this_does_not_prove: the baseline and the judge's rubric were written by the same assistant, so agreement between them is not independent evidence that either is right. The owner's grades supersede the baseline wherever they are given, and the gate in the review tool is recomputed from the owner's grades alone.

adv0053.summary: Asks how 'my MP' voted on the assisted dying bill without saying who that is or naming a constituency.
adv0053.why: A sound ambiguity trap: there is genuinely no referent, and the forbidden claim forbids exactly the failure mode, guessing a member or constituency.

adv0018.summary: Asserts Parliament voted in September 2026 to lift the fracking ban; the evidence is a Reform member arguing the case for fracking in a debate on the ban.
adv0018.why: The premise is false in the right way: the record holds a debate, the forbidden claim names the invented vote, and the evidence shows the debate that makes the confusion tempting.

adv0020.summary: Asserts NATS blamed a cyber-attack; the minister's reply says a cyber-attack has been ruled out and points to a technical issue at Swanwick.
adv0020.why: The evidence contradicts the premise in the speaker's own words, so a system that falls for the framing can be caught on the record rather than on opinion.

adv0024.summary: Asserts the Liberal Democrats voted against the medical training bill; Helen Morgan's own words put her amendments alongside her party's overall support for it.
adv0024.why: The correction is in the cited sentence, and the forbidden claim names the exact false assertion.

adv0061.summary: Loaded question assuming the Government is letting China spy from Royal Mint Court; the evidence is the planning minister saying the decision rests with Planning Ministers, independent of the rest of Government.
adv0061.why: Both vital nuggets separate what the record holds from what the questioner assumes, which is what a loaded-framing item has to do to be scoreable.

adv0014.summary: Asks what the inquiry chair told MPs; the record has an MP describing the community giving him a standing ovation, not him speaking.
adv0014.why: A clean mention-versus-speaker trap: he is named in the Chamber but never speaks in it, and the forbidden claim covers any words put in his mouth.

adv0015.summary: Asks what a broadcaster said in the Commons; the words quoted in the record are his social media post read out by an MP.
adv0015.why: The speaker of record is Greg Smith, so the attribution the question invites is exactly what the forbidden claim rules out.

adv0009.summary: Attributes 'holiday tax' to the Chancellor; the phrase is Rebecca Paul's, from the Conservative benches.
adv0009.why: The evidence carries the phrase in the real speaker's mouth, and I saw the same speech again in the calibration sample, so the attribution is solid.

adv0043.summary: Asks what annual revenue the Government said the overnight visitor levy would raise; the levy is debated repeatedly but no Government revenue figure appears.
adv0043.why: I checked all five near-miss sentences: the only figures are a critic's Oxford Economics cost estimate and 'any money raised' with no number, so the abstention holds.

adv0044.summary: Asks what the Prime Minister said in the Westminster Hall debate on water ownership; the Prime Minister did not speak in it.
adv0044.why: The single near-miss sentence points at a different Westminster Hall debate, on social enterprises and community ownership, so nothing in the record supports an answer.

adv0049.summary: Asks what Nigel Farage said in the fracking ban debate; the Reform contribution in the record is Richard Tice's.
adv0049.why: No sentence in the corpus carries the question's terms together, and the party-level confusion it baits is a real one.

old0023.summary: Asks what the Government said about funding a new Antarctic research station; the topic is absent from the record.
old0023.why: Zero near-miss sentences, so it is trivially abstained, but the brief keeps one of these three as a sanity check and this is the cleanest of them.

old0024.summary: Asks what was said about licensing the UK's first spaceport launch, and forbids any answer at all on the ground that the topic is not in the record.
old0024.why: The record DOES speak to it: a 2024 Commons sentence says SaxaVord became the UK's first licensed vertical-launch spaceport, so a correct sourced answer would be scored as a harmful fabrication.

old0025.summary: Asks what the Minister said about UK plans for lunar exploration missions; the topic is absent from the record.
old0025.why: Zero near-miss sentences and no lunar material anywhere in the corpus, so the abstention is safe.

adv0032.summary: Asks whether an MP said her constituents can switch water company; she said the opposite, which is why she backs public ownership.
adv0032.why: The polarity flip is on the record in one sentence, which is what makes a negation-flip item scoreable rather than arguable.

adv0034.summary: Asks whether Richard Burgon said he would support the Government's amendment; he said he would vote against it.
adv0034.why: His own sentence states the opposite of the premise, and neither of the two decoy passages the pool retrieved for this question contains him at all.

adv0026.summary: Inflates 2,000 cancelled flights to 20,000; the record says over 2,000, with more than 150,000 passengers affected.
adv0026.why: An order-of-magnitude perturbation against a figure that is verbatim in the evidence, so confirming it is unambiguously wrong.

adv0027.summary: Inflates the OBR's 1.8 billion pound digital ID estimate to 18 billion; the minister's words give the real figure.
adv0027.why: A decimal-point perturbation with the true figure and its source both in the cited sentence, which the calibration sample independently confirmed.

adv0039.summary: Asks what MPs said about the Grenfell Tower fire in the week it happened, which was June 2017, outside every window this corpus covers.
adv0039.why: Sound as a test but the question never states the year, so the automatic window check cannot confirm it and a system has to supply the date from world knowledge.

adv0042.summary: Asks what MPs said in the days after the death of Queen Elizabeth II in September 2022, which is outside the corpus windows.
adv0042.why: The date is stated in the question, so being out of window is checkable, and the forbidden claim rules out any fabricated tribute.

adv0001.summary: Asks whether the minister said a cyber-attack caused the disruption; he said a cyber-attack had been ruled out.
adv0001.why: The words of the question are present in the passage with the opposite polarity, which is the hardest form of this trap and the one worth keeping.

adv0051.summary: Asks what 'the Prime Minister' said about economic growth across a record that spans four different Prime Ministers.
adv0051.why: A genuine ambiguity in this corpus rather than a contrived one, and the calibration sample showed a passage naming a later Prime Minister, which confirms the span.

hum0089.summary: A colloquial question about the cost of the Chagos deal, whose evidence mentions the Chagos islands only in passing inside an argument about digital ID spending.
hum0089.why: A good near-miss, but it is typed as expected_behaviour 'answer' while its own vital nugget says the answer is not there, because the colloquial category forces 'answer'.

adv0019.summary: Asserts the Government cancelled the Chinese embassy application; the minister says the decision rests with Planning Ministers, independent of the rest of Government.
adv0019.why: The premise is contradicted by the cited sentence, and the pool's decoys for this question were all about the espionage case, which is the confusion the item probes.

adv0021.summary: Asserts a peer praised the education statement; she called it the worst she had heard in 33 years.
adv0021.why: The reversal is verbatim in her own sentence, so the item cannot be argued with.

adv0022.summary: Asserts the Lords threw out the medical training bill; the record has them debating amendments to it.
adv0022.why: The evidence shows the Bill alive in committee, which is what makes the invented rejection detectable from the record.

adv0023.summary: Asserts the Government apologised in the Commons for Flybe's collapse; the cited contributions describe the job losses and ask what will be done.
adv0023.why: No apology appears anywhere in the quoted material, and the forbidden claim names the fabrication precisely.

adv0025.summary: Asserts an amendment of Rebecca Paul's to scrap the visitor levy was defeated; her contribution is a speech against the levy, with no amendment in it.
adv0025.why: Confirmed twice over: the evidence is a speech, and the calibration passage from the same debate likewise contains no amendment.

adv0057.summary: Asks why the Government 'caved in' on its 'disastrous' reorganisation plans; a Liberal Democrat member said only that the Government had finally listened, too late.
adv0057.why: Both loaded words are isolated in a vital nugget as the questioner's, and the record's actual words are in the evidence to answer with instead.

adv0058.summary: Asks why Labour is determined to tax family holidays; the minister presented the levy as empowering local leaders to invest.
adv0058.why: The item separates an imputed intent from what the Government actually said, and the evidence carries the Government's own framing.

adv0060.summary: Asks why MPs keep ignoring women 'robbed' of pensions; the Commons debated the ombudsman's report and the evidence describes work done by the APPG and the ombudsman.
adv0060.why: It refuses both halves of the framing, the factual claim of neglect and the characterisation, each in its own vital nugget.

adv0062.summary: Asks whether scrapping jury trials is obviously an attack on justice; members argued both that delay denies justice and that reducing jury trial is wrong.
adv0062.why: Two forbidden claims, one for the conclusion and one for the word 'scrapping', which is the right structure for a contested proposal.

adv0016.summary: Asks what a chief constable told the House; he was named by the policing minister, and police officers do not speak in the Chamber.
adv0016.why: The vital nugget gives the structural reason rather than just the fact, which is what makes this trap generalise.

adv0017.summary: Asks what Margaret Thatcher said in the Venezuela debate; she was quoted by Ed Davey in 2026, having died in 2013.
adv0017.why: The quotation really is in the record under Ed Davey's name, which I saw in the calibration sample, so the trap works on a genuine retrieval hit.

adv0008.summary: Attributes the Swanwick explanation to the Leader of the Opposition; it was given by a minister for the Government.
adv0008.why: The evidence is the real speaker's technical explanation, and the pool's decoys for this question were her speeches on other subjects, exactly the bait the item is built on.

adv0011.summary: Attributes a point about MI5 and GCHQ assessments to Ed Davey; it was made by the security minister.
adv0011.why: The evidence carries the real speaker's words, and the calibration sample confirmed Ed Davey's retrieved speech is about Venezuela.

adv0045.summary: Asks what the Government said the Rosebank consultation concluded; the record has the consultation closing but no stated conclusion.
adv0045.why: No sentence carries the question's terms together, and the calibration passage on Rosebank has the minister explicitly declining to comment on the merits.

adv0046.summary: Asks what compensation the Government offered WASPI women in that debate; the debate is on the ombudsman's report and offers no figure.
adv0046.why: I read all five near-miss sentences: they call for compensation and note uncertainty about funding, but none carries a Government offer or an amount.

adv0035.summary: Asserts Wendy Morton put the islands' future with the UK Government alone; she tied it to the islanders' wishes.
adv0035.why: Her own sentence states the opposite, and the calibration sample showed the Government side saying the same thing, so the record is consistent.

adv0028.summary: Reduces almost 89,000 lost hospitality jobs to 89; the evidence gives the real figure.
adv0028.why: A thousand-fold perturbation on a figure that is verbatim in the record, and the calibration sample found a peer citing 90,000 for the same claim, which is a difference worth noting but does not weaken the trap.

adv0029.summary: Asks whether the high-risk vendor cap is 55%; the minister's sentence says high-risk vendors are limited to a minority presence of up to 35%.
adv0029.why: The correcting figure is inside the cited quote, so the item is self-contained even though the quote is long.

adv0031.summary: Asks whether 300 people in total lost their jobs at Flybe; the record says about 2,000 in total, of whom about 300 were in Scotland.
adv0031.why: The hardest kind of numeric trap, a real figure with the wrong scope attached, and both numbers sit in the same cited sentence.

adv0002.summary: Asserts an MP said the evidence base showed lower-volume fracking was safe; she said Ministers claim the evidence is not there and pressed them on it.
adv0002.why: The polarity is reversed inside a single sentence of the evidence, which I also graded in the calibration sample as the passage that states both sides.

adv0003.summary: Asserts a member said benefits are not paid for by taxpayers; he said they are paid by the taxpayers of today or tomorrow.
adv0003.why: The cited sentence is the exact inversion of the premise, and the decoy the pool retrieved for this question contains neither the speaker nor the claim.

adv0004.summary: Asserts a member said businesses had plenty of time before laying people off; he said they saw no choice but to lay off workers now.
adv0004.why: The evidence contradicts the premise in the speaker's own words, with the urgency explicit.

hum0067.summary: Asks whether the Government supports public ownership of water; the evidence is a Labour backbencher stating her own support.
hum0067.why: The most valuable attribution test in the set, but like hum0089 it is typed 'answer' while its vital nugget says the passage does not carry a Government position.

k:db0229:FE814B4C-480B-471E-BA22-00D3985.summary: A tabled Commons oral question from Charlotte Nichols asking what steps are being taken to support UK nationals overseas who are at risk from covid-19.
k:db0229:FE814B4C-480B-471E-BA22-00D3985.why: Same broad subject (covid-19 in the Commons in March 2020) but a different debate on a different date, and a tabled question text cannot show who led off.

k:adv0028:9B711AFF-432C-4488-8925-57A9BA.summary: A Conservative peer attacks the Government's record on retail and hospitality and cites UKHospitality's figure of 90,000 hospitality jobs lost since the 'jobs tax'.
k:adv0028:9B711AFF-432C-4488-8925-57A9BA.why: It carries the figure the question mis-states, 90,000 rather than 89, said by a Conservative, so it settles the question but amid a great deal of other material.

k:old0016:B47910BF-7E9B-428A-8C1C-C73736.summary: Perran Moon asks Treasury Ministers to work with the business department to make Cornwall an industrial strategy zone.
k:old0016:B47910BF-7E9B-428A-8C1C-C73736.why: It is the right member raising a matter, but at Topical Questions rather than Business questions, so it does not answer the question as scoped (this is I-38).

k:hum0084:F57473E2-3D02-41D6-ACB3-5A2CA4.summary: A Liberal Democrat MP argues that the only purpose of a mandatory ID is to let people be asked for it, which turns a free society into a permissions-based one.
k:hum0084:F57473E2-3D02-41D6-ACB3-5A2CA4.why: It answers 'what is the point' directly, but only from the opposing side and as an intervention put to another member rather than an account of the case for ID.

k:old0010:204C3F87-A77C-45C3-9487-26F65C.summary: A Conservative peer presses the Minister on a million young people not in work or training, and claims employment costs have depressed entry-level hiring.
k:old0010:204C3F87-A77C-45C3-9487-26F65C.why: The claim is being put TO the Minister by an opposition peer, so the passage shows the claim being made and not whether the Government accepts it.

k:hum0061:73DB31DE-AEE9-4EB1-83A0-F4BDDD.summary: An MP warns about the cumulative effect on Jewish people of banning Maccabi Tel Aviv fans, and asks why other clubs' rioting fans are treated differently.
k:hum0061:73DB31DE-AEE9-4EB1-83A0-F4BDDD.why: It is one of the two debates the question compares, but nothing in the text says which came first in the record.

k:adv0003:ADF2E167-241B-4F1B-ACDE-D13D2D.summary: A Conservative peer argues that lifting children out of poverty takes more than extending benefits, because some children are let down by money and others by the adults around them.
k:adv0003:ADF2E167-241B-4F1B-ACDE-D13D2D.why: Same subject area as the question (benefits and child poverty) but it contains neither Sir Ashley Fox nor any claim that benefits are not paid for by taxpayers.

k:hum0094:D1F48822-8116-4D69-AC64-D4FE42.summary: A Liberal Democrat MP contrasts the 4.6 billion already spent on the cancelled 2010 ID card scheme with the 1.8 billion cost attached to digital ID.
k:hum0094:D1F48822-8116-4D69-AC64-D4FE42.why: It supplies one of the three things asked for, the cost figure, but not who produced it nor whether the Government accepts it.

k:db0263:0B30E1F2-C7EA-4FE4-AB06-E975C76.summary: A Green MP asks the Minister when business rates will be reformed, citing village pubs in his constituency facing large increases.
k:db0263:0B30E1F2-C7EA-4FE4-AB06-E975C76.why: Different debate, date and subject: nothing here touches a debate on vicars and rural parishes.

k:hum0064:A7B12CF1-8E28-48F9-B2A7-4B0E56.summary: A Liberal Democrat MP criticises moving asylum seekers between unsuitable accommodation and sets out his party's plan to end hotel use in six months.
k:hum0064:A7B12CF1-8E28-48F9-B2A7-4B0E56.why: It does contrast Government and Liberal Democrat positions, but on asylum accommodation, not on local government reorganisation.

k:hum0067:2E207C29-FF61-40ED-B65C-3B781A.summary: A Labour backbencher opens a petition debate arguing that water privatisation has failed and that full public ownership is needed.
k:hum0067:2E207C29-FF61-40ED-B65C-3B781A.why: Squarely on the subject, but it is a backbencher's case for public ownership and says nothing about whether the Government supports it.

k:adv0020:9B6D9923-C1DC-4669-966E-C2133D.summary: A minister says NATS has confirmed the disruption was a technical issue and does not believe it was cyber-related, while assuring the House about cyber defences.
k:adv0020:9B6D9923-C1DC-4669-966E-C2133D.why: It is about exactly this matter and states the fact that settles the question: NATS blamed a technical fault, not a cyber-attack.

k:hum0100:D5E05B8F-C93B-4890-8CDA-A0678F.summary: The Deputy Speaker notifies the House of Royal Assent to three Acts: unauthorised entry to football matches, sentencing, and Holocaust memorial.
k:hum0100:D5E05B8F-C93B-4890-8CDA-A0678F.why: On the subject of bills completing their passage in 2026, but the Crime and Policing Bill is simply not in the list, so it settles nothing.

k:adv0027:5003558C-5263-4847-BB68-7D86CF.summary: A Conservative MP attacks digital ID as inconsistent and insecure, and says the OBR reckons the scheme will cost 1.8 billion pounds while Ministers brief that this is inaccurate.
k:adv0027:5003558C-5263-4847-BB68-7D86CF.why: It attributes the cost to the OBR and gives the real figure, 1.8 billion rather than 18, but inside a long speech about many other things.

k:db0240:744F89D1-DAC4-491A-94B8-3FD6F60.why: Wrong House, wrong date and wrong debate; the only link to the question is the word 'business'.

k:db0294:668E6111-A05A-40B5-A940-3B5B6AF.why: It is from the very sitting the division belongs to and identifies the Bill, but it never mentions the division or the reasoned amendment.

k:hum0017:DBB2A7A3-44E9-4C0D-B095-514C59.why: It mentions meeting a farmer, but the speaker is an MP rather than a peer and the subject is land classification, not whether reforms can be paid for.

k:db0297:B69E4125-15E0-40AD-9A98-1EA68CF.why: A different debate eight days earlier, with no division in it.

k:hum0029:BC5F82C7-0294-4989-8FEF-E715B5.summary: The Security Minister responds to the collapse of the Official Secrets Act prosecution, welcoming the committee's report and saying it found no evidence of ministerial interference.
k:hum0029:BC5F82C7-0294-4989-8FEF-E715B5.why: The right speaker on this row, making a point about the security committees' findings, though about the prosecution rather than the embassy.

k:db0252:76C141E6-3271-45FD-A1DF-5B31060.summary: An MP raises a proposed 1,900-acre solar and battery scheme spanning his constituency.
k:db0252:76C141E6-3271-45FD-A1DF-5B31060.why: Wrong House, subject and year; craftspeople and EU travel are absent.

k:db0258:7CA8292E-DD1F-48D3-829E-666CD46.summary: A Labour MP argues in a 2020 Budget debate that regional inequality must be central to economic strategy.
k:db0258:7CA8292E-DD1F-48D3-829E-666CD46.why: Shares only the word 'economy'; there is no Office for the Impact Economy here.

k:db0261:15B71995-709A-4264-84A9-4EDFD91.summary: A Conservative MP asks how to get press coverage for backbench debates, citing an excellent Ukraine debate initiated by Sir Bernard Jenkin on 4 December.
k:db0261:15B71995-709A-4264-84A9-4EDFD91.why: It does name who initiated a Ukraine debate, but the wrong one on the wrong date, which is exactly the trap.

k:db0232:348E5375-6AF4-46E5-9203-A6670EC.summary: A Labour MP speaks on NHS workforce pressure and cancer care, thanking local fundraisers.
k:db0232:348E5375-6AF4-46E5-9203-A6670EC.why: Health in general, but nothing about the Infected Blood Inquiry's recommendations.

k:db0229:8700473C-87F4-4500-ACF9-6141884.summary: A peer asks whether the shared prosperity fund's objectives will survive covid-19, especially for inner cities.
k:db0229:8700473C-87F4-4500-ACF9-6141884.why: Wrong House and debate; 'covid-19' appears only as a passing qualifier.

k:hum0002:9DCEC254-582B-48D8-B996-A60704.summary: An energy minister says he cannot comment on the merits of Jackdaw and Rosebank, and that the Secretary of State will decide on consent in due course.
k:hum0002:9DCEC254-582B-48D8-B996-A60704.why: The right minister on the Rosebank consents, but the passage never says what the Scottish courts did to them.

verdict.verdict: usable for recall, MRR and binary nDCG; NOT for graded nDCG

gate.applies_to: binarised relevance at grade >= 2, which is what recall, MRR and nDCG read
gate.meaning: the binarised gate decides whether the judge may be used for ranking metrics at all; the four-level one decides only whether graded nDCG may be reported
